editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Trade With No Bali PMA Route
editorial.standfirst: Retail musical-instrument trade is open to full foreign ownership nationally, yet Bali blocks PMA registration for the activity under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Retail musical-instrument trade is a category with a pleasingly broad retail vocabulary. It covers the sale of instruments from Indonesia’s traditional repertoire—kecapi, bamboo flute, calung, angklung, kolintang, gamelan set, rebab, rebana, tifa and sasando—alongside modern instruments including saxophone, harmonica, trombone, guitar, mandolin, ukulele, harp, bass, violin, cello, piano, organ and drums. The inclusion of tuning forks makes the perimeter especially clear: the activity is about musical instruments and their retail presence, not a narrow genre or a single tradition. Its scope lets traditional and modern instruments sit under the same retail roof without asking the business to choose between them.

The registration scales are uncomplicated: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open to this activity. That gives the category one consistent description across those listed scales. The important qualifier is geographical, not a difference in the kind of instrument being sold. A shop centred on bamboo flutes and angklung, or one offering guitars, pianos and drums, falls within the stated retail scope; its scale can be any of the four listed.

At the national level, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. That is an unambiguous national ceiling: a foreign investor may hold the full ownership interest nationally. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. But national status alone does not settle the answer on the island. The Bali register marks the activity Blocked (risk class), so a foreigner cannot register it in Bali today as PMA.

The reason is specific. At Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, and Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities from PMA registration. Therefore, the national 100% ownership ceiling remains a national fact, while the Bali outcome is a block on PMA registration. It is a clear distinction worth preserving: full national foreign ownership does not create a Bali PMA route for this retail activity under the stated moratorium.
